pos: n. (Peter Bulkeley, 1583–1659, founder and pastor of Concord, Massachusetts, author of The Gospel-Covenant)
etymology: English surname Bulkeley, from a Cheshire place name, the bullock clearing; Greek Petros, a stone.
biblical_def: Peter Bulkeley was rector of Odell in Bedfordshire for twenty-one years, silenced for nonconformity by Archbishop Laud's visitation, and emigrated in 1635. With Simon Willard he led the company that settled Concord, and he was its pastor until his death, spending a considerable private fortune on the town and its poor. His The Gospel-Covenant; or The Covenant of Grace Opened, preached at Concord and printed in London in 1646, is among the earliest full treatments of covenant theology written in America: it sets out the covenant of works made with Adam, the covenant of grace in Christ, the conditions and the absoluteness of the promise, and the duties of a people in covenant. He sat in the synod of 1637 that judged the antinomian teaching of Anne Hutchinson. Neh 9:38 is the act his theology is built around, a people who “make a sure covenant, and write it” (Neh 9:38).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a covenant as a mutual agreement, and in theology, the covenant of grace, in which God promises salvation on condition of faith in Christ.
webster_full: COV'ENANT, n. In theology, the covenant of works is that implied in the commands, prohibitions, and promises of God; the covenant of redemption and grace is that by which God engages to bestow salvation on man, upon the condition that man shall believe in Christ.
GRACE, n. The free unmerited love and favor of God, the spring and source of all the benefits men receive from him.
PROM'ISE, n. In a Scriptural sense, a declaration of the divine will, assuring to men some good or deliverance.
scriptures: Neh 9:38
And because of all this we make a sure covenant, and write it; and our princes, Levites, and priests, seal unto it.

And if it seem evil unto you to serve the LORD, choose you this day whom ye will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were on the other side of the flood, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land ye dwell: but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.
Eph 1:4
According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love:
Rom 9:16
So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy.
corruption_summary: He spent a fortune on a frontier town and wrote America's first great book on the covenant.
corruption_paragraphs: Bulkeley's book is a useful corrective to the caricature of New England covenant theology as a legal scheme. He holds the absolute freeness of the promise — Eph 1:4, election before the foundation of the world, and Rom 9:16, that it is “not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth” (Rom 9:16) — and from that very freeness derives the covenant duties, because the covenant God makes is with a people He has chosen and whom He therefore binds.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the written covenant. Neh 9:38 has a people set their names to an engagement, and Jos 24:15 has Joshua force the choice into words, “as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD” (Jos 24:15). New England churches were gathered this way and the practice has nearly vanished; a modern congregation commonly has a membership roll and no covenant, which is a list without an engagement. Bulkeley's part in the 1637 synod shows the other side of covenant seriousness: a church that has bound itself to a doctrine must act when the doctrine is denied from within.
roots_summary: Hebrew berith (H1285), a covenant; 'amanah (H548), a sure agreement; Greek eklegomai (G1586), to choose out.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'amanah (H548) — a covenant, sure agreement; Nehemiah 9:38.
Greek eklegomai (G1586) — to choose out, elect; Ephesians 1:4.
usage: “we make a sure covenant, and write it” (Neh 9:38) — the act his book expounds.
“as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD” (Jos 24:15) — the choice put into words.
“not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth” (Rom 9:16) — the freeness underneath the bond.

pos: n. (Nathaniel Ward, c. 1578–1652, minister of Ipswich, Massachusetts, drafter of the Body of Liberties and author of The Simple Cobler of Aggawam)
etymology: English surname Ward, a watchman, guard; Hebrew Nethane'l, gift of God.
biblical_def: Nathaniel Ward practised law before he entered the ministry, was excommunicated for nonconformity in 1633, and came to Massachusetts, where he served the church at Agawam, afterwards Ipswich. His legal training was put to the colony's use: the General Court commissioned him to draw a body of laws, and the Massachusetts Body of Liberties adopted in 1641 is substantially his work, the first code of fundamental law enacted in English America. He also wrote The Simple Cobler of Aggawam in America, printed in London in 1647, a pungent and much-quoted attack on religious toleration, on England's political disorder, and on the fashions of the age. He returned to England and died as rector of Shenfield. Deu 17:19 is the standard he held out to magistrates, that the ruler shall read the law “all the days of his life” (Deu 17:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a liberty as a privilege or immunity enjoyed by prescription or grant, and a code as a collection or digest of laws.
webster_full: LIB'ERTY, n. Privilege; exemption; immunity enjoyed by prescription or by grant; as the liberties of the commercial cities of Europe.
CODE, n. A collection of the laws and constitutions of a nation or state; a digest or compilation of laws by public authority.
COB'LER, n. A mender of shoes; a clumsy workman; a mender of any thing.
scriptures: And it shall be with him, and he shall read therein all the days of his life: that he may learn to fear the LORD his God, to keep all the words of this law and these statutes, to do them:
Pro 29:2
When the righteous are in authority, the people rejoice: but when the wicked beareth rule, the people mourn.
Rom 13:4

For he is the minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil.
Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
corruption_summary: A lawyer-minister wrote English America's first code of laws, and a famous tract against tolerating anybody.
corruption_paragraphs: Ward's code is a real achievement and the dictionary honours it: written fundamental law, limits on the magistrate, guarantees of trial, restraints on arbitrary imprisonment, and penalties grounded in Scripture rather than in the will of the court. Deu 17:19 requires a ruler who reads the law continually, and Rom 13:4 gives the sword a defined purpose, to execute wrath on evildoers rather than to act at pleasure. Pro 29:2 names what is at stake for the people under either sort of ruler.

The Simple Cobler is where honest naming is required. Ward argued against liberty of conscience as such, holding that the magistrate must suppress error, and the dictionary rejects that position for the reasons set out in the entries on Murton and Busher: the sword does not produce faith, and compulsion fills a church with hypocrites. His wit has kept the tract in print and his argument lost in the English-speaking world within a century and a half, partly to men whose own books he would have had suppressed. Isa 8:20 is the proper weapon against error, the law and the testimony, not the constable.
roots_summary: Hebrew qara (H7121), to read, call; mishpat (H4941), judgment; Greek machaira (G3162), sword.
roots_lines: Hebrew qara (H7121) — to read aloud, call; Deuteronomy 17:19.
Hebrew mashal (H4910) — to rule, have dominion; Proverbs 29:2.
usage: “he shall read therein all the days of his life” (Deu 17:19) — his standard for magistrates.
“When the righteous are in authority, the people rejoice” (Pro 29:2) — what is at stake.
“To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20) — the proper weapon against error.

pos: n. (the Massachusetts Body of Liberties, 1641, the first code of fundamental law enacted in English America)
etymology: English body, a collected whole, from Old English bodig; liberties, privileges and immunities, from Latin libertas.
biblical_def: The Body of Liberties was adopted by the General Court of Massachusetts in December 1641 after nearly a decade of pressure from the deputies, who wanted the colony's law written down rather than left to the discretion of magistrates. Drafted chiefly by Nathaniel Ward, its hundred clauses guarantee that no man's life, honour, or estate shall be taken but by express law or the word of God, forbid torture to compel confession except in limited cases, require juries, limit the courts, protect the property of married women and the rights of servants, forbid cruelty to beasts, and set out the liberties of the churches. Clause ninety-one declares that there shall never be bond slavery among the colonists except for lawful captives taken in just wars and those who sell themselves, and that such shall have the liberties of the Hebrew servant law. Deu 17:19 and Pro 31:9 are the two texts the whole instrument serves.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines fundamental as essential, serving for the foundation, and a statute as an act of the legislature, a written law.
webster_full: FUNDAMENT'AL, a. Pertaining to the foundation or basis; serving for the foundation; essential; important.
STAT'UTE, n. An act of the legislature of a state that extends its binding force to all the citizens or subjects of that state; a written law.
SERV'ANT, n. A person hired to perform the business of another; one who is in subjection or bondage.
scriptures: And it shall be with him, and he shall read therein all the days of his life: that he may learn to fear the LORD his God, to keep all the words of this law and these statutes, to do them:
Pro 31:9
Open thy mouth, judge righteously, and plead the cause of the poor and needy.
And he that stealeth a man, and selleth him, or if he be found in his hand, he shall surely be put to death.
Deu 24:7
If a man be found stealing any of his brethren of the children of Israel, and maketh merchandise of him, or selleth him; then that thief shall die; and thou shalt put evil away from among you.
corruption_summary: A hundred written liberties, and one clause that left a door open which later generations drove through.
corruption_paragraphs: The code's achievement is that it exists. Before 1641 a Massachusetts colonist's security depended on the character of the magistrate; after it, on a written instrument he could read. The requirement that nothing be imposed but by express law or the word of God is a remarkable double standard of restraint, and Pro 31:9 states the duty it encodes: “Open thy mouth, judge righteously, and plead the cause of the poor and needy” (Pro 31:9).

The corruption is clause ninety-one, and the dictionary names it rather than celebrating around it. By excepting lawful captives of just wars and men who sell themselves, the clause provided the legal opening through which chattel slavery entered New England, and Massachusetts became the first English colony to give slaveholding statutory recognition. Exo 21:16 fixes a capital penalty on the man who steals and sells a man, and Deu 24:7 repeats it; the exception for captives cannot be stretched to cover the Atlantic trade, and within a generation it was being so stretched. A written liberty is only as good as its narrowest clause.
roots_summary: Hebrew mishpat (H4941), judgment; ganab (H1589), to steal; 'ebed (H5650), a servant, bondman.
usage: “judge righteously, and plead the cause of the poor and needy” (Pro 31:9) — the duty encoded.
“he that stealeth a man, and selleth him” (Exo 21:16) — what clause ninety-one let in.
“he shall read therein all the days of his life” (Deu 17:19) — why law is written down.

pos: n. (Thomas Dudley, 1576–1653, four times governor of Massachusetts Bay, signer of the Harvard charter)
etymology: English surname Dudley, from the Worcestershire place name, Dudda's clearing.
biblical_def: Thomas Dudley came to Massachusetts in 1630 as deputy governor under Winthrop and served the colony for twenty-three years, four of them as governor and thirteen as deputy. He was the hardest of the founding magistrates: he pressed for written law against Winthrop's preference for magisterial discretion, prosecuted the antinomian party, and opposed every proposal for toleration. He founded Newtown, afterwards Cambridge, signed Harvard's charter, and was the father of the poet Anne Bradstreet. A paper found in his pocket after his death carried the lines he meant for his own epitaph, warning men of God in courts and churches to watch over such as do a toleration hatch. Psa 2:10 is the text his whole magistracy was conducted under, “Be wise now therefore, O ye kings: be instructed, ye judges of the earth” (Psa 2:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a governor as one invested with supreme authority in a state or colony, and a charter as a written instrument conferring rights and privileges.
webster_full: GOV'ERNOR, n. One who governs; one invested with supreme authority; the supreme magistrate of a state or colony.
CHAR'TER, n. A written instrument, executed with usual forms, given as evidence of a grant, contract, or whatever is done between man and man.
DEP'UTY, n. A person appointed or elected to act for another, especially a person sent with a special commission to act in the place of another.
scriptures: Psa 2:10
Be wise now therefore, O ye kings: be instructed, ye judges of the earth.
Psa 2:11
Serve the LORD with fear, and rejoice with trembling.
Pro 29:2
When the righteous are in authority, the people rejoice: but when the wicked beareth rule, the people mourn.

And if it seem evil unto you to serve the LORD, choose you this day whom ye will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were on the other side of the flood, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land ye dwell: but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.
corruption_summary: He wanted the colony's law written down, and he wanted no toleration in it.
corruption_paragraphs: Dudley was right about one thing and wrong about another, and the two were connected. He was right that discretionary magistracy is dangerous, and his pressure is a chief reason the Body of Liberties was written at all; Pro 29:2 is a practical observation about what rule without restraint does to a people. Psa 2:11 adds the posture he genuinely held, to “Serve the LORD with fear, and rejoice with trembling” (Psa 2:11), which is more than a formula in a man who gave up an English estate for a frontier.

He was wrong that the magistrate's commission extends to suppressing religious error, and the dictionary says so. The entries on Murton and Busher set out the reasons; here it is enough to note that the same instinct which produced a written code also produced the banishments, and that a colony which wrote liberties for servants and beasts would not write one for conscience. Jos 24:15 puts the choice of whom to serve to a household and a people and leaves it there, as a choice, which is precisely what Dudley's epitaph would not allow.
roots_summary: Hebrew sakal (H7919), to be prudent, wise; yacar (H3256), to instruct, chasten; bachar (H977), to choose.
roots_lines: Hebrew sakal (H7919) — to be wise, prudent; Psalm 2:10.
usage: “Be wise now therefore, O ye kings” (Psa 2:10) — the text of his magistracy.
“Serve the LORD with fear, and rejoice with trembling” (Psa 2:11) — his real posture.
“as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD” (Jos 24:15) — left as a choice.

pos: n. (John Norton, 1606–1663, teacher of the First Church in Boston, author of The Orthodox Evangelist)
etymology: English surname Norton, from the north farmstead or settlement.
biblical_def: John Norton came to New England in 1635, served Ipswich with Nathaniel Ward, and succeeded John Cotton as teacher of the First Church in Boston. He was the colony's chief controversialist. His The Orthodox Evangelist (1654) is a systematic treatment of the person of Christ, the covenant, and effectual calling; he answered William Pynchon's book denying that Christ suffered the penal wrath of God, and his Discussion of the Great Point in Divinity, the Sufferings of Christ is a defence of penal substitution against the view that the atonement was a transaction of obedience only. He wrote the first American life of a minister, of Cotton, and in 1662 went with Simon Bradstreet as the colony's agent to Charles II. He also wrote in defence of the capital laws against the Quakers, under which four were hanged. Gal 1:8 is the text he applied freely, and 1Jn 4:1 the duty he discharged.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines orthodox as sound in the Christian faith, and substitution as the act of putting one person or thing in the place of another.
webster_full: OR'THODOX, a. Sound in the Christian faith; believing the genuine doctrines taught in the Scriptures; opposed to heretical.
SUBSTITU'TION, n. The act of placing one person or thing in the place of another, to supply its want.
SAT'ISFACTION, n. That which satisfies; amends; atonement; payment; indemnification for an injury.
scriptures: Gal 1:8
But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.
Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world.
Tit 1:11
Whose mouths must be stopped, who subvert whole houses, teaching things which they ought not, for filthy lucre's sake.
Also of your own selves shall men arise, speaking perverse things, to draw away disciples after them.
corruption_summary: He defended penal substitution ably and defended the gallows for Quakers, and the dictionary separates the two.
corruption_paragraphs: Norton's answer to Pynchon is the valuable half of him. Pynchon had argued that Christ did not bear the Father's penal wrath but offered a perfect obedience which God accepted; Norton showed that this empties the satisfaction of its content, since a penalty not borne is a penalty remitted without payment. The dictionary holds substitutionary penal atonement, and Norton's treatise is one of the earliest American defences of it. 1Jn 4:1 commands the trying of spirits and Gal 1:8 supplies the seriousness of the verdict where another gospel is in view.

His defence of the capital laws against the Quakers must be named as the error it was, and naming it is not a concession to modern sentiment but an application of the same Scripture. The magistrate's sword in Rom 13:4 is for evildoers in the civil order; a man's return to a colony that has banished him for his religion is not a crime against person or property. Four Quakers were hanged in Boston between 1659 and 1661, and the colony later repented of it. Tit 1:11 says of false teachers that their “mouths must be stopped” (Tit 1:11) — stopped by sound doctrine, which is the instrument Paul names in the same chapter, not by execution.
roots_summary: Greek anathema (G331), accursed; dokimazo (G1381), to try; epistomizo (G1993), to stop the mouth.
roots_lines: Greek anathema (G331) — accursed, devoted to destruction; Galatians 1:8.
Greek epistomizo (G1993) — to stop the mouth, silence; Titus 1:11.
usage: “let him be accursed” (Gal 1:8) — the verdict on another gospel.
“try the spirits whether they are of God” (1Jn 4:1) — the duty he discharged well.
“Whose mouths must be stopped” (Tit 1:11) — by doctrine, not by the gallows.

pos: n. (Urian Oakes, c. 1631–1681, minister of Cambridge, Massachusetts, and president of Harvard College)
etymology: English surname Oakes, a dweller by the oaks; Urian, a form of the Welsh Urien.
biblical_def: Urian Oakes was brought to New England as a child, graduated from Harvard in 1649, ministered in England at Titchfield until the Act of Uniformity ejected him in 1662, and returned to be pastor of the church at Cambridge, Massachusetts. From 1675 he acted as president of Harvard and from 1680 held the office outright until his death the next year, serving the pulpit and the college together. His published sermons include New-England Pleaded With, the election sermon of 1673, and The Unconquered Christian, a funeral sermon for Thomas Shepard the younger; he also wrote an elegy on Shepard that is among the better poems produced in the colony. He was a Latin orator of real power and a defender of the strict congregational way against the loosening of membership. 1Co 16:13 is the charge his election sermon pressed on the colony.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an elegy as a mournful or plaintive poem, and an election sermon as one preached at the annual choice of magistrates.
webster_full: EL'EGY, n. A mournful or plaintive poem, or a funeral song; a poem or a song expressive of sorrow and lamentation.
PRES'IDENT, n. An officer appointed or elected to preside over a corporation, company or assembly of men.
ORA'TION, n. A speech or discourse composed according to the rules of oratory, and spoken in public.
scriptures: Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong.
I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith:
Let us hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering; (for he is faithful that promised;)
Pro 9:10
The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom: and the knowledge of the holy is understanding.
corruption_summary: He held a pulpit and a college at once, and spent his best sermon telling New England it was declining.
corruption_paragraphs: The election sermon was New England's annual institution for saying to the magistrates what the ministers thought, and Oakes used his to argue that the colony was losing the thing it had been founded for. The charge was not that the churches had fallen into open sin but that the second generation held the covenant as an inheritance rather than a profession. 1Co 16:13 is the summons he pressed: “Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong” (1Co 16:13).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the joining of the college to the pulpit. Oakes presided over Harvard while pastoring Cambridge, and Pro 9:10 gives the premise on which that combination makes sense: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom” (Pro 9:10), so that a college is not a neutral institution with a chaplain attached. Heb 10:23 and 2Ti 4:7 are what he preached at funerals and what was preached at his, after six years of holding two full offices and dying at about fifty.
roots_summary: Greek gregoreo (G1127), to watch; andrizomai (G407), to act like a man; Hebrew chokmah (H2451), wisdom.
roots_lines: Greek gregoreo (G1127) — to watch, be vigilant; 1 Corinthians 16:13.
Greek andrizomai (G407) — to act the man, be courageous; 1 Corinthians 16:13.
usage: “quit you like men, be strong” (1Co 16:13) — the election sermon's charge.
“The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom” (Pro 9:10) — why a college needs a creed.
“I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course” (2Ti 4:7) — two offices, fifty years.

pos: n. (John Higginson, 1616–1708, minister of Salem, Massachusetts, for forty-eight years)
etymology: English patronymic Higgin-son, son of Higgin, a diminutive of Richard.
biblical_def: John Higginson was the son of Francis Higginson, the first minister of Salem, and came to New England as a boy of thirteen in 1629. He served as chaplain at Saybrook and minister at Guilford, and in 1660 was settled over the church at Salem, where he remained until his death in 1708, forty-eight years in the pulpit his father had opened. He preached the election sermon of 1663, The Cause of God and His People in New-England, and wrote the attestation that stands at the front of Cotton Mather's Magnalia Christi Americana, commending the preservation of the colony's history. He was almost ninety when the Salem witchcraft prosecutions ran through his own parish and his own daughter was among those cried out upon. Heb 13:7 is the duty he spent his old age discharging, that the church remember those who spoke to it the word of God.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an attestation as testimony, witness, and a chronicle as a historical account of facts in the order of time.
webster_full: ATTESTA'TION, n. Testimony; witness; a solemn or official declaration in support of a fact.
CHRON'ICLE, n. An historical account of facts or events disposed in the order of time; a register.
PAS'TORATE, n. The office, state or jurisdiction of a spiritual pastor.
scriptures: Heb 13:7
Remember them which have the rule over you, who have spoken unto you the word of God: whose faith follow, considering the end of their conversation.
Psa 78:4
We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, and his strength, and his wonderful works that he hath done.
Surely he shall not be moved for ever: the righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance.

And I heard a voice from heaven saying unto me, Write, Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord from henceforth: Yea, saith the Spirit, that they may rest from their labours; and their works do follow them.
corruption_summary: Forty-eight years in his father's pulpit, and the witchcraft terror came through it at the end.
corruption_paragraphs: Higginson is the connecting thread of Salem's whole century: his father opened the church in 1629 and he closed his own ministry there in 1708. His attestation to the Magnalia argues that a church must write its history down or lose the evidence of God's dealings with it, which is Psa 78:4 made into a programme: “We will not hide them from their children” (Psa 78:4).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the weight of a long settled pastorate, which Psa 112:6 describes as a righteous man not moved, in “everlasting remembrance” (Psa 112:6). The trial of his last years belongs in the record: the 1692 prosecutions reached into his own household when his daughter was accused, and the spectral evidence on which the court proceeded was afterwards repudiated by the colony and by the ministers who had failed to stop it in time. Heb 13:7 asks the reader to consider the end of a teacher's conversation, and Higginson's end was to watch his parish do the worst thing it ever did.
roots_summary: Greek mnemoneuo (G3421), to remember; Hebrew kachad (H3582), to hide; zeker (H2143), remembrance.
roots_lines: Greek anastrophe (G391) — manner of life, conversation; Hebrews 13:7.
usage: “We will not hide them from their children” (Psa 78:4) — his argument for writing history.
“the righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance” (Psa 112:6) — a long pastorate's weight.
“considering the end of their conversation” (Heb 13:7) — and his end was Salem, 1692.

pos: n. (the church covenant subscribed at Salem, Massachusetts, 6 August 1629, the first in New England)
etymology: Hebrew shalem, peace, whence the town's name; Latin convenire, to come together, agree.
biblical_def: The Salem Covenant was subscribed on 6 August 1629 by about thirty persons who gathered themselves into a church at Salem, with Francis Higginson as teacher and Samuel Skelton as pastor. It is one sentence: that they covenant with the Lord and one with another, and bind themselves in the presence of God to walk together in all His ways, according as He is pleased to reveal Himself unto them in His blessed word of truth. It is the earliest church covenant in New England and the model for hundreds that followed. In 1636 an enlarged form was added, a renewal in seven articles against specific sins the congregation confessed, which became the pattern for later covenant renewals. Neh 9:38 is the act in Scripture that it imitates, a people who “make a sure covenant, and write it” (Neh 9:38).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a covenant as a mutual agreement, and to subscribe as to sign with one's own hand, to attest by writing the name.
webster_full: COV'ENANT, n. A mutual consent or agreement of two or more persons, to do or to forbear some act or thing; a contract; stipulation.
SUBSCRI'BE, v.t. To sign with one's own hand; to give consent to something written, by signing the name.
RENEW'AL, n. The act of renewing; the act of forming anew; renovation.
scriptures: Neh 9:38
And because of all this we make a sure covenant, and write it; and our princes, Levites, and priests, seal unto it.

They clave to their brethren, their nobles, and entered into a curse, and into an oath, to walk in God's law, which was given by Moses the servant of God, and to observe and do all the commandments of the LORD our Lord, and his judgments and his statutes;

And if it seem evil unto you to serve the LORD, choose you this day whom ye will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were on the other side of the flood, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land ye dwell: but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.

And the king stood by a pillar, and made a covenant before the LORD, to walk after the LORD, and to keep his commandments and his testimonies and his statutes with all their heart and all their soul, to perform the words of this covenant that were written in this book. And all the people stood to the covenant.
corruption_summary: One sentence, thirty names, and the pattern for every New England church after it.
corruption_paragraphs: The brevity is the point. The covenant does not enumerate doctrines; it binds the subscribers to walk together in all God's ways as He shall reveal them from His word, which commits them in advance to obedience they cannot yet foresee. That is the same undertaking the Gainsborough and Scrooby companies made, and it is what distinguishes a gathered church from a parish: membership begins with an act of the member. Neh 10:29 describes the Israelites who “entered into a curse, and into an oath, to walk in God's law” (Neh 10:29).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is covenant renewal. The 1636 addition is a confession of named sins followed by a fresh engagement, which is what 2Ki 23:3 records of Josiah and the people standing to the covenant. Modern congregations rarely do either part; a membership class is not an oath, and a vision statement is not a confession of named sins. Jos 24:15 shows the choice being pressed on a people until they say the words themselves.
roots_summary: Hebrew berith (H1285), a covenant; 'alah (H423), an oath, curse; 'amad (H5975), to stand.
usage: “we make a sure covenant, and write it” (Neh 9:38) — Salem, 6 August 1629.
“entered into a curse, and into an oath, to walk in God's law” (Neh 10:29) — the weight of it.
“And all the people stood to the covenant” (2Ki 23:3) — the pattern for renewal.

pos: n. (the Massachusetts synod of 1679–80 which named the colony's provoking evils and adopted the Savoy Declaration)
etymology: Latin reformare, to form again; Greek sunodos, a meeting, an assembly come together.
biblical_def: The Reforming Synod met at Boston in September 1679 and again in May 1680, called by the General Court to answer two questions: what are the evils that have provoked the Lord to bring His judgments on New England, and what is to be done that those evils may be reformed. Increase Mather was its moving spirit and drafted its result, printed as The Necessity of Reformation, which named thirteen heads of provoking evil — decay of godliness in professors, pride, neglect of church fellowship, profanity and Sabbath-breaking, failure of family government, intemperance, want of truth among neighbours, inordinate affection to the world, opposition to the work of reformation, and want of public spirit. The second session adopted a confession of faith, the Savoy Declaration with small changes, as the churches' doctrinal standard. 2Ki 23:3 is the act it called for, a people standing to the covenant.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a synod as an ecclesiastical council, and reformation as correction or amendment of life, manners, or of any thing vicious or corrupt.
webster_full: SYN'OD, n. A council or meeting of ecclesiastics to consult on matters of religion; an ecclesiastical council.
REFORMA'TION, n. The act of reforming; correction or amendment of life, manners, or of any thing vicious or corrupt.
PROVO'KE, v.t. To call into action; to arouse; to excite; to anger; to offend.
scriptures: And the king stood by a pillar, and made a covenant before the LORD, to walk after the LORD, and to keep his commandments and his testimonies and his statutes with all their heart and all their soul, to perform the words of this covenant that were written in this book. And all the people stood to the covenant.

They clave to their brethren, their nobles, and entered into a curse, and into an oath, to walk in God's law, which was given by Moses the servant of God, and to observe and do all the commandments of the LORD our Lord, and his judgments and his statutes;
Act 15:6
And the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter.
Jas 1:27
Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.
corruption_summary: A synod asked what evils had provoked God, wrote thirteen of them down, and adopted a confession.
corruption_paragraphs: The synod's method is what makes it useful and uncomfortable. It did not issue a general call to repentance; it enumerated specific sins, several of them sins of the respectable — inordinate affection to the world, want of truth among neighbours, failure of family government, and opposition to reformation itself. Jas 1:27 supplies the test the list keeps returning to, that pure religion is to visit the afflicted and “to keep himself unspotted from the world” (Jas 1:27).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is naming sins by name. A church that confesses in generalities never has to change anything in particular. 2Ki 23:3 and Neh 10:29 both show the engagement being made specific and public, and Act 15:6 shows the elders gathering to consider a matter rather than circulating a statement. The synod's adoption of the Savoy Declaration in its second session is the complementary half: a church that means to reform must say what it believes, since the evils named in the first session were failures measured against a standard.
roots_summary: Hebrew berith (H1285), covenant; 'amad (H5975), to stand; Greek sunodos, an assembly come together.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'amad (H5975) — to stand, take one's stand; 2 Kings 23:3.
usage: “And all the people stood to the covenant” (2Ki 23:3) — the act the synod called for.
“to keep himself unspotted from the world” (Jas 1:27) — the test behind the thirteen heads.
“the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter” (Act 15:6) — the form.

pos: n. (the constitution adopted by the churches of Connecticut at Saybrook in 1708, establishing consociations and associations)
etymology: From Saybrook, Connecticut, named for Lords Say and Brooke; platform, a plan or scheme, from French plateforme.
biblical_def: The Saybrook Platform was drawn up by delegates of the Connecticut churches at Saybrook in September 1708 and enacted by the colony's General Court the same year. It has three parts: it adopted the Savoy Declaration as the churches' confession of faith; it received the Heads of Agreement, the English scheme of union between Presbyterians and Congregationalists; and it added fifteen articles of its own establishing county consociations of churches with power to determine cases of discipline, and ministerial associations to examine and license candidates. Its effect was to move Connecticut congregationalism toward a presbyterian settlement, giving standing bodies above the particular church a real jurisdiction. It governed the colony's churches until the nineteenth century. The question it raises is the one John Wise had argued in Massachusetts three years earlier: whether Mat 18:17 leaves the last earthly word with the congregation.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a consociation as an association, a union of churches, and a platform as a plan, a scheme, a form of government.
webster_full: CONSOCIA'TION, n. Intimate union; fellowship; a union of churches by their pastors and delegates; a meeting of the pastors and delegates of a number of churches.
PLAT'FORM, n. A plan; a scheme; the sketch of a plan; in church affairs, an ecclesiastical constitution.
ASSOCIA'TION, n. Union; connection; a society formed for the transaction of business, or for promoting some object.
scriptures: And if he shall neglect to hear them, tell it unto the church: but if he neglect to hear the church, let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican.
Act 15:6
And the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter.
Let all things be done decently and in order.
Let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double honour, especially they who labour in the word and doctrine.
corruption_summary: Connecticut gave standing councils of churches real jurisdiction, and became presbyterian in all but name.
corruption_paragraphs: The Platform's motive was order, and the disorder it answered was real: isolated frontier churches with no recourse in a disputed discipline case, and candidates examined by nobody in particular. Act 15:6 shows apostles and elders coming together to consider a matter, and 1Co 14:40 requires that all things be done decently and in order, so consultation among churches is not the error.

The error is jurisdiction. The Platform's consociations did not advise; they determined, and a church that refused their determination could be declared no longer in communion. That transfers the last earthly word in discipline from the congregation to a standing court, and Mat 18:17 puts it in the congregation: “tell it unto the church” (Mat 18:17). The dictionary holds local-church congregational governance and therefore reads Saybrook as a departure, taken for good reasons, which within a century had produced in Connecticut a body indistinguishable in practice from a presbytery. 1Ti 5:17 honours ruling elders within the church, not above a company of churches.
roots_lines: Greek parakouo (G3878) — to neglect to hear; Matthew 18:17.
usage: “tell it unto the church” (Mat 18:17) — where the last earthly word belongs.
“came together for to consider of this matter” (Act 15:6) — consultation is not the error.
“Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40) — the disorder it answered.
